\[
\hat{f} = \arg\min_f\ \tfrac{1}{2} \lVert h * f - g \rVert^2 + \lambda \sum_{x} \lvert \nabla f(x) \rvert,
\qquad
p \leftarrow \frac{p + \sigma \nabla \bar{f}}{\max(1,\, \lvert p + \sigma \nabla \bar{f} \rvert / \lambda)},
\quad
f' = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\mathcal{F}(f + \tau \operatorname{div} p) + \tau \overline{H}\, \mathcal{F} g}{1 + \tau \lvert H \rvert^2}\right),
\quad
\bar{f} = 2 f' - f,
\qquad
\lambda = 3,\ K = 100
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(g\): The blurred image extended with the border mode
- \(f\): The estimate of the sharp image
- \(h, H\): The PSF and its Fourier transform
- \(p\): The dual field, one 2-D vector per pixel
- \(\lambda\): The weight of the total variation term
- \(\tau, \sigma\): The primal and dual step sizes, both 1 / sqrt(8)

The filter looks for the image f whose blurred copy h * f is close to the photo g. Many images fit a blurred photo, and most are full of noise. The total variation term, the sum of the gradient length over all pixels, picks the one with the least jumping around. Rudin, Osher and Fatemi used this term to remove noise. It keeps sharp edges, since one edge costs the same as a slow ramp of the same height. The sum has no gradient where the image is flat, so the filter uses the primal-dual algorithm of Chambolle and Pock. A dual field p, one 2-D vector per pixel, lives in the disk of radius lambda. Each step moves p along the gradient of the extrapolated image f bar and pulls it back into the disk. Then f moves along the divergence of p, and the data term is solved exactly with the FFT. H is the transform of the PSF. The steps tau and sigma are both 1 / sqrt(8), since the squared norm of the gradient is at most 8. Differences wrap around at the edges of the extended image. The first estimate is the photo, and p starts at 0. The PSF is the same as for Richardson-Lucy.
